summary: Describes how the DES cipher in Cipher Block Chaining mode, with an explicit initialization vector, provides confidentiality inside IPsec's Encapsulating Security Payload. DES is now considered too weak for modern use. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: It describes a way of locking packet contents in a secret code so only the right receiver can read them. The lock it uses is an old one that is now easy to pick.

questions: how does des-cbc work in esp
what is the esp des-cbc cipher
why must ipsec ivs be random
subtitle: How IPsec ESP can encrypt packets with DES in CBC mode, carrying a fresh random IV in every packet.

tldr.problem: ESP needs a cipher to keep packet contents confidential, and each packet must be decryptable even if others are lost or reordered.
tldr.mechanism: DES in Cipher Block Chaining mode with 8-octet blocks and a 64-bit key. Every packet carries an explicit random 8-octet IV right before the encrypted payload.
tldr.outcome: The RFC itself warns that DES is not a good choice for even moderate-value information against a determined attacker, and suggests Triple DES. It also strongly discourages using the cipher without authentication.

today: RFC 2405 is a Proposed Standard published in November 1998, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. The RFC itself already cautions that DES is weak and that Triple DES is probably a better choice.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2405 describes using the DES cipher in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode, with an explicit initialization vector, as the confidentiality mechanism in the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP). DES is a symmetric block cipher, defined in FIPS documents the RFC cites.

As specified here, DES-CBC is not an authentication mechanism. The RFC mentions DES-MAC as one that does provide authentication but does not discuss it. How the pieces of ESP fit together is covered in RFC 2406 and RFC 2411.
sections.eli5: This describes how to scramble the contents of a packet so only the right receiver can read it. It only hides things. It does not check who sent them.

sections.title: Algorithm and Mode
sections.content:
DES-CBC is a symmetric secret-key block algorithm with a block size of 64 bits. In CBC mode, each block is chained to the one before it, so identical plaintext blocks do not produce identical ciphertext.

For speed, the RFC reports that Phil Karn tuned DES-CBC software to achieve 10.45 Mbps on a 90 MHz Pentium, scaling to 15.9 Mbps on a 133 MHz Pentium.
sections.eli5: The message is cut into small chunks. Each chunk is mixed with the scrambled chunk before it, so the same words never look the same twice.

sections.title: The ESP Payload and IV
sections.content:
DES-CBC needs an explicit Initialization Vector (IV) of 8 octets (64 bits). The IV immediately precedes the protected, encrypted payload, and it MUST be a random value. Because each datagram includes its own IV, every received datagram can be decrypted even if some datagrams are dropped or reordered in transit.

The RFC gives an implementation note. Common practice is to use random data for the first IV and the last 8 octets of encrypted data from one encryption as the IV for the next, which logically extends CBC across packets. Whichever way is used, the receiver MUST NOT assume any meaning for the value other than that it is an IV. Implementations MUST NOT use a counter or other low-Hamming-distance source for IVs, to avoid ECB encryption of very similar plaintext blocks in different packets.

The block size is 8 octets (64 bits). When padding is needed, it MUST follow the conventions of RFC 2406.
sections.eli5: Every packet comes with its own random starting twist written on the front. That way the receiver can unlock any packet by itself, even if others get lost.

sections.title: Key Material and Weak Keys
sections.content:
The DES key size is 64 bits. It is commonly known as a 56-bit key because only 56 bits are significant; the least significant bit of every byte is a parity bit. The key derivation mechanism from RFC 2401 MUST derive a 64-bit key value. It produces raw key values and is not responsible for parity or weak key checks. A strong pseudo-random function MUST be used to generate the key, as discussed in RFC 1750.

Weak key checks SHOULD be performed. If a weak key is found, it SHOULD be rejected and a new SA requested. DES has 16 known weak keys, including so-called semi-weak keys, and the known weak keys have been adjusted for parity.

On key lifetime, the RFC cites brute-force estimates: for a cost of $300,000, a 56-bit DES key could be recovered in an average of 19 days with off-the-shelf technology and in only 3 hours with a custom chip. It makes no specific lifetime recommendation, saying the right lifetime depends on the perceived threat relative to the worth of the data.
sections.eli5: The key is a short secret number. A few keys are known to be bad, so you skip them. A determined, well-funded attacker can try every key, which is why the lock is considered weak.

sections.title: Interaction with Authentication Algorithms
sections.content: The RFC states that, as of writing, no known issues prevent DES-CBC from being used with any specific authentication algorithm. This matters because the Security Considerations strongly discourage using the cipher without authentication. The RFC says it can be used in an ESP transform that includes authentication, or in one without it provided there is a companion AH header (see RFC 2402).
sections.eli5: The lock can be paired with any kind of signature check, and the RFC says you really should pair them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security depends completely on the strength of DES, correct implementations, the SA management mechanism, the key, and every participating node. The RFC describes a cut-and-paste splicing attack that applies to all CBC algorithms and can be addressed with an authentication mechanism, so using the cipher without authentication is strongly discouraged.

The attacks are described bluntly. A differential cryptanalysis attack needs 2^47 plaintext-ciphertext pairs and a linear cryptanalysis attack needs 2^43 pairs; neither is considered practical. But Wiener designed a DES-cracking machine costing $1 Million that can crack one key every 3.5 hours, which the RFC calls an extremely practical attack. One or two blocks of known plaintext suffice, and IP datagrams typically begin with known or guessable header text, so frequent key changes will not help.

The RFC suggests DES is not a good algorithm for even moderate-value information against such equipment, and that Triple DES is probably better. It still argues that ESP DES-CBC gives far more privacy than sending cleartext. It also quotes Steve Bellovin on why IVs must be random: with a counter-like IV, the effective plaintext of the first block barely changes between packets, giving cryptanalysts a wedge.
sections.eli5: The RFC admits that someone with a very expensive machine could break the lock, so use a stronger one for valuable things. Even so, it is much better than sending a postcard anyone can read.
